paragraphs: Sequential observations are dependent: the next state of a random walk depends on its current state. This paper establishes a concentration bound for averages of Hermitian matrices attached to states visited by a finite Markov chain. The chain must be aperiodic and irreducible. Under these conditions, the bound controls the extreme eigenvalues of the average, with tail probabilities decreasing exponentially.

The authors apply this result to co-occurrence matrices, which summarize which states appear together in sequential data. For a chain with n states and mixing time t, a trajectory of length O(t(log(n) + log(t))/e²) suffices to estimate the co-occurrence matrix within error e. This connects the amount of data required to the chain's mixing behavior and the desired accuracy.

Experiments are consistent with the predicted exponential convergence. The contribution therefore combines a general matrix concentration result with a concrete sample requirement for sequential statistics. The authors identify this as the first convergence-rate bound for co-occurrence matrices and the first sample-complexity analysis in graph representation learning.
neurips-2020-a-matrix-chernoff-bound-for.tldr: A matrix concentration bound for finite Markov chains establishes how much sequential data suffices to estimate co-occurrence matrices accurately.

paragraphs: This paper studies swap regret, a performance measure for algorithms that make decisions repeatedly. The measure matters in repeated-game theory and is closely connected to correlated equilibria. The paper addresses both the best regret rate that algorithms can hope to achieve and how to construct algorithms that control this measure efficiently.

Its first result is a lower bound of Ω(√(TN log N)), where T counts decision rounds and N counts available actions. The bound is tight up to a constant factor, resolving an open problem about the achievable rate. This establishes a fundamental performance barrier: improvements cannot remove this dependence on rounds and actions beyond constant factors in the setting studied.

The second contribution is a computationally efficient conversion from algorithms with no external regret to algorithms with no swap regret. The reduction applies in both full-information and bandit settings and improves on previous regret bounds. Together, the results clarify the theoretical limit while supplying a practical algorithmic route for transferring existing regret guarantees to the swap-regret setting.
neurips-2020-a-tight-lower-bound-and-eff.tldr: The paper establishes a tight swap-regret lower bound and an efficient reduction that converts no-external-regret algorithms into no-swap-regret algorithms.

paragraphs: A loss function determines how a learning algorithm penalizes its mistakes. Rather than choosing that function in advance, this paper studies learning a loss alongside the predictive model. The aim is to adapt the loss to the domain while retaining the mathematical structure of proper losses, a class grounded in statistics and Bayesian decision theory.

Previous approaches learn a canonical link, a monotonic function relating probabilities to real-valued scores, and obtain a proper loss through integration. The authors use a broader formulation of proper composite losses based on source functions from information geometry. Fitting these functions eases constraints encountered when fitting canonical links directly.

The technical construction transforms squared Gaussian processes into a random process whose paths satisfy the requirements for source functions. This provides a structured way to learn suitable functions rather than treating loss selection as an unconstrained search. Experiments report substantial improvements over the state of the art, supporting the usefulness of this more flexible route to learning losses.
neurips-2020-all-your-loss-are-belong-to.tldr: The paper learns proper loss functions through source functions and a Gaussian-process construction, reporting substantial improvements over prior methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies uncertainty estimates from a two-layer neural network whose first-layer weights are random and whose second layer is trained with ridge regularization. The analysis considers growing sample size, input dimension, and hidden-layer width, with dimension-to-sample and width-to-sample ratios approaching finite limits.

Under Gaussian features, Lipschitz activations, and a linear regression response allowing possibly nonlinear perturbations, a weighted average of network derivatives becomes asymptotically normally distributed. The authors use this result to construct confidence intervals for individual components of the unknown regression vector. Thus, derivatives of a nonlinear trained network provide a route to frequentist uncertainty quantification under the stated model.

The analysis also finds a double-descent pattern in interval length: for certain fixed input-dimension ratios, intervals first widen and then narrow as the width-to-sample ratio grows. This connects network size to the precision of inference, beyond prediction error alone. A numerical toolbox predicts interval lengths and supports comparisons of activation functions and other parameters.
neurips-2020-asymptotic-normality-and-co.tldr: For a specified random-feature neural network model, asymptotic derivative distributions yield confidence intervals whose lengths can exhibit double descent.

paragraphs: Fairness assessments often compare numerical measures across protected demographic groups. When only a small number of examples have labels, those comparisons can be uncertain. This paper asks how abundant unlabeled examples can help estimate group fairness more reliably, rather than relying exclusively on the limited labeled sample.

The proposed Bayesian framework uses a hierarchical latent-variable model conditioned on labeled examples to estimate calibrated scores for unlabeled examples within each group. These scores support inference about several fairness metrics. Instead of returning only a single estimate, the framework produces posterior distributions that express uncertainty about the values of those metrics.

Across multiple fairness datasets, sensitive attributes, and predictive models, the authors report significant, consistent reductions in estimation error. They also describe estimates as more accurate and less variable than methods using labeled data alone. The contribution concerns the reliability of fairness measurement: combining the two kinds of data can provide stronger evidence about a model's group-level behavior while retaining an explicit representation of uncertainty.
neurips-2020-can-i-trust-my-fairness-met.tldr: A Bayesian framework combines scarce labeled examples with abundant unlabeled data to estimate group fairness more accurately and quantify uncertainty.

paragraphs: Images of the same subject can look very different when captured through different sensing modalities, making alignment difficult. CoMIR learns dense, image-like representations that retain information shared across modalities. Aligning these representations turns the original multimodal registration problem into one that can use ordinary intensity-based or feature-based registration algorithms.

Training requires aligned images and a separate neural network for each modality. A contrastive objective based on InfoNCE teaches the networks to produce shared representations. The authors modify that objective without adding hyperparameters to enforce rotational equivariance: the representation should respond consistently when an image rotates, a property needed for registration.

The study assesses rotational behavior and representation stability using RGB and near-infrared remote-sensing images. It then evaluates registration on bright-field and second-harmonic generation microscopy images, which have little apparent correlation. On that biomedical evaluation, CoMIR significantly outperforms representations produced through GAN-based image translation and an application-specific method using additional data knowledge. These results support learning shared spatial information as a useful route to multimodal alignment.
neurips-2020-comir-contrastive-multimoda.tldr: CoMIR learns shared image representations that let conventional registration algorithms align visually different imaging modalities.

paragraphs: A system learning tasks sequentially faces two different needs. It should preserve earlier knowledge when a new task is unrelated, and reuse useful knowledge when tasks are similar. This paper addresses sequences containing both types, bringing protection against forgetting and knowledge transfer into the same network.

The proposed algorithm automatically detects whether an incoming task resembles any earlier tasks. For dissimilar tasks, it focuses on limiting forgetting. For similar tasks, it selectively transfers knowledge from relevant previous tasks to improve learning of the new one. Selectivity matters because the sequence can contain a mixture of useful and unrelated prior experience.

The paper also frames backward transfer, where later learning can help earlier models, as part of the combined capability it seeks to provide. Its empirical evaluation uses mixed task sequences and demonstrates the proposed model's effectiveness. The central contribution is therefore a continual-learning approach that responds to task relationships, rather than treating every new task as requiring the same balance between preserving and sharing knowledge.
neurips-2020-continual-learning-of-a-mix.tldr: The method automatically detects task similarity to combine forgetting prevention with selective knowledge transfer in mixed continual-learning sequences.

paragraphs: Models with binary latent variables are difficult to train because their gradients can be hard to estimate accurately. Continuous relaxations offer one route, but are not always available. The ARM estimator instead introduces continuous auxiliary randomness and uses antithetic sampling to obtain an unbiased gradient estimate with relatively low variance.

This paper identifies a tension within ARM: antithetic sampling reduces variance, while introducing auxiliary randomness increases it. DisARM analytically integrates out randomness introduced by the augmentation process. The authors establish a substantial variance reduction from this change, while retaining the same computational cost as ARM and a simple implementation.

On several generative-modeling benchmarks, DisARM consistently improves both gradient variance and log-likelihood relative to ARM and a strong independent-sample baseline. The authors also develop a local version for optimizing a variational bound that uses multiple samples, reporting improvements over VIMCO. The work shows how removing analytically manageable randomness can improve learning without increasing the estimator's computational cost.
neurips-2020-disarm-an-antithetic-gradie.tldr: DisARM removes auxiliary randomness from ARM gradient estimates, reducing variance at the same computational cost and improving generative-model benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why collecting more experience does not always correct mistakes in Q-learning. With function approximation and bootstrapped targets, the training-data distribution can interact with value estimates in a harmful way. New observations may fail to provide corrective feedback, potentially causing instability, suboptimal convergence, and difficulty learning from noisy, sparse, or delayed rewards.

DisCor addresses this issue by optimizing the distribution used to train the value function. Its goal is to emphasize data that can correct accumulated value-estimation errors. The algorithm computes a tractable approximation to a distribution that optimally induces corrective feedback, yielding sample weights based on the estimated accuracy of target values.

The resulting approach changes how existing training examples influence learning. Experiments report substantial improvements across challenging reinforcement-learning settings, including learning multiple tasks and learning with noisy reward signals. These findings support corrective feedback as a useful design principle for training distributions, while the analysis identifies a possible failure mechanism rather than claiming to explain every source of reinforcement-learning instability.
neurips-2020-discor-corrective-feedback-.tldr: DisCor reweights reinforcement-learning samples according to estimated target accuracy to encourage correction of accumulated value-function errors.

paragraphs: A classifier can satisfy a fairness criterion on its training distribution yet lose that property when the distribution changes. This paper studies fairness across a specified family of changes formed by reweighting training samples. Its target is a classifier that remains fair throughout that family while also controlling prediction loss.

The authors formulate a min-max objective combining distributionally robust loss minimization with fairness across the distribution class. They reduce the problem to finding a fair classifier robust to those distributions and develop an iterative method based on online learning. The algorithm is proved to converge to such a fair and robust solution.

Experiments on standard fairness datasets suggest that the method preserves fairness guarantees and test accuracy across a broad set of test-set perturbations compared with existing fair classifiers. The experiments also reveal a trade-off between fairness robustness and accuracy. The contribution extends fairness beyond a single empirical distribution, with protection tied specifically to the perturbation class considered rather than to arbitrary changes in deployment data.
neurips-2020-ensuring-fairness-beyond-th.tldr: The paper develops classifiers with fairness guarantees across sample-reweighting perturbations and studies the associated trade-off with accuracy.

paragraphs: Sampling can make graph convolutional network training more scalable by limiting the neighborhoods processed at each step. However, preparing and loading fresh samples introduces overhead, especially when memory and bandwidth become bottlenecks. This paper examines sampling frequency as a separate design choice from the strategy used to select nodes.

LazyGCN samples periodically and reuses the selected nodes between sampling operations. The framework is designed to work with any sampling strategy, allowing existing methods to reduce repeated data preparation. The central idea is that every training step need not require a newly prepared sample for training to remain effective.

The theoretical analysis obtains the same convergence rate as the underlying sampling method under a mild condition on recycling size, through reduced variance in inner layers. Experiments on large real-world graphs support the approach: it substantially reduces sampling steps and improves speed without sacrificing accuracy in the reported evaluations. The contribution connects algorithmic sampling decisions to the systems costs that can otherwise erode their expected scalability benefits.
neurips-2020-gcn-meets-gpu-decoupling-wh.tldr: LazyGCN accelerates graph-network training by periodically sampling and reusing nodes, with a conditional guarantee of the underlying method's convergence rate.

paragraphs: Reducing numerical precision can shrink neural networks and accelerate inference, but very low precision can damage accuracy. Mixed precision assigns more bits to sensitive layers, creating an exponentially large set of possible assignments. HAWQ-V2 improves a Hessian-based approach for navigating this choice using second-order information about the network.

The paper theoretically establishes average Hessian trace as the appropriate sensitivity metric, replacing a heuristic based only on the largest eigenvalue. It also introduces automatic bit selection through a Pareto-frontier method, removing manual assignment of layer precisions. A further contribution extends Hessian-based analysis to mixed-precision activations, which the authors find especially beneficial for object detection.

The authors report state-of-the-art results across tasks, including automatically selected quantization for InceptionV3, ResNet50, and SqueezeNext. On Microsoft COCO detection, they report gains of 2.6 mAP over direct uniform quantization and 1.6 over FQN, with a smaller model size of 17.9 MB. These results support using richer sensitivity information and automated precision allocation to balance model size and accuracy.
neurips-2020-hawq-v2-hessian-aware-trace.tldr: HAWQ-V2 uses Hessian-trace sensitivity and automatic precision selection to improve mixed-precision quantization of neural-network weights and activations.

paragraphs: A fairness rule applied to decisions today does not by itself explain how a population will fare over time. This paper studies the interaction between algorithmic decisions and changes in group qualification. It uses a partially observed Markov decision framework to represent dynamics in which relevant population states are not fully observed.

The authors characterize equilibria of these dynamics to examine whether static fairness constraints improve group well-being and reduce inequality over the long term. Their results are conditional: the same broad type of constraint can promote equality or worsen disparities. The outcome depends on what drives qualification transitions and how sensitive attributes influence feature distributions.

The paper also considers interventions that can improve group qualification or promote equality between groups. Its evidence combines theoretical analysis with experiments using static real-world datasets and simulated dynamics. This makes the framework a tool for studying possible long-term effects, rather than direct evidence of observed population trajectories. The central lesson is that evaluating fairness over time requires modeling the processes through which qualification changes.
neurips-2020-how-do-fair-decisions-fare-.tldr: A dynamic model shows that static fairness constraints can improve or worsen long-term group equality depending on qualification transitions and feature distributions.

paragraphs: Representing professional hockey players is difficult because there are many players and some participate only sparsely. A model must learn from uneven amounts of experience while accounting for different playing contexts. This paper develops player representations within a Markov game model tailored to sequential ice-hockey data.

A variational encoder represents player information through latent variables. It learns a shared prior that depends on context, drawing individual posterior representations toward shared information through shrinkage. This allows players with different participation levels to benefit from statistical information across the population. The proposed Variational Recurrent Ladder Agent Encoder, or VaRLAE, adds a hierarchy of latent variables to model play dynamics and prevent latent posterior collapse.

Evaluation uses a dataset containing more than 4.5 million events. The authors report state-of-the-art performance in identifying the acting player, estimating expected goals, and predicting final score difference. These results support contextualized representations as useful inputs to multiple sports-analysis tasks, while addressing the particular challenge of learning about players with limited observations.
neurips-2020-learning-agent-representati.tldr: VaRLAE learns contextual hockey-player representations that share information across uneven participation levels and improve three sports-analytics tasks.

paragraphs: A representation can retain useful information without making that information accessible to the predictor that will use it. This paper studies optimal representations for supervised learning with the downstream predictive family explicitly in view. It argues that representation quality should be tied to generalization and the chosen decoder, such as a linear classifier.

The Decodable Information Bottleneck adapts the information-bottleneck approach by measuring information retention and compression from that decoder's perspective. Traditional information bottlenecks compress inputs while preserving target information without accounting for a particular decoder. DIB instead links those goals to what the desired family of predictors can decode.

Within this framework, the authors characterize representations that are optimal for expected test performance and can be estimated with guarantees. Empirically, they show that DIB can encourage a small gap between training and test performance for downstream classifiers and help predict neural-network generalization. The contribution is a decoder-dependent account of useful representation learning, connecting the structure of learned information to the predictive model expected to use it.
neurips-2020-learning-optimal-representa.tldr: The Decodable Information Bottleneck defines useful representations relative to a chosen predictive family and connects them to expected test performance.

paragraphs: Image classifiers are often tested for robustness by adding synthetic changes such as noise or simulated weather. This paper asks whether success on those tests carries over to differences that arise naturally between datasets. The distinction matters because robustness to an artificial perturbation does not automatically establish robustness to real-data variation.

The authors evaluate 204 ImageNet models under 213 test conditions. Across this testbed, they find that robustness to synthetic shifts often transfers little or not at all to natural shifts. Most of the techniques examined do not provide robustness to the natural distribution changes included in their evaluation.

Training with larger and more diverse datasets is the main exception: it improves robustness in multiple cases. Even those improvements leave substantial performance gaps. The findings therefore call for evaluating natural shifts directly and treating them as an unresolved research problem. Their scope is the models, techniques, and conditions studied, rather than a universal claim that synthetic robustness can never help with naturally changing data.
neurips-2020-measuring-robustness-to-nat.tldr: A large ImageNet evaluation finds that robustness to synthetic perturbations often fails to transfer to natural dataset shifts.

paragraphs: Memory-based meta-learning trains agents to adapt quickly across tasks drawn from a target distribution. A prior theoretical argument suggested that this training encourages Bayes-optimal behavior. This paper investigates that explanation empirically on prediction and bandit tasks, asking whether the resemblance extends beyond agents making similar decisions.

The authors compare the agents' computational structure using an approximate simulation relationship: one agent system can approximately simulate the other. Their results indicate that meta-learned and Bayes-optimal agents share internal computational organization as well as behavior. They also show that Bayes-optimal agents are fixed points of the meta-learning dynamics.

These findings suggest that memory-based meta-learning can serve as a numerical method for approximating Bayes-optimal agents. The authors propose that this could be useful even for task distributions lacking tractable models. That broader possibility is an implication of the results, while the empirical investigation concerns the prediction and bandit tasks examined. The work provides evidence for a computational explanation of rapid adaptation through meta-training.
neurips-2020-meta-trained-agents-impleme.tldr: Experiments find behavioral and computational similarities between meta-trained and Bayes-optimal agents, supporting meta-learning as a possible numerical approximation method.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning homogeneous halfspaces, classifiers whose separating boundary passes through the origin, when labels may contain adversarial noise. It uses the agnostic, distribution-specific PAC setting, comparing the learned classifier with the best-fitting halfspace. The benchmark error, called opt, allows for labels that no halfspace can classify perfectly.

For a broad structured family of input distributions, including log-concave distributions, the authors prove that non-convex stochastic gradient descent efficiently reaches misclassification error O(opt) + ε. This means the error is controlled by a constant multiple of the best halfspace's error, plus an additional accuracy term. The guarantee depends on the specified distribution family.

The paper contrasts this result with a lower bound for convex surrogate optimization: any such surrogate can inherently lead to error ω(opt), even with Gaussian input marginals. This establishes a separation between the analyzed non-convex approach and convex surrogate objectives. The significance is that an easier-looking optimization objective can lose classification guarantees that a suitable non-convex method retains in this noisy learning setting.
neurips-2020-non-convex-sgd-learns-halfs.tldr: Under structured input distributions, non-convex SGD learns noisy halfspaces with error guarantees that convex surrogate optimization cannot match.

paragraphs: Topic models discover themes in collections of documents, but approaches centered on word occurrences can overlook semantic relationships between words. This paper introduces an optimal-transport framework that incorporates those relationships through the geometry of word embeddings. The aim is to learn topics whose words fit together more meaningfully.

The method uses optimal transport to exploit the spatial structure of semantically related words in embedding space. This gives semantic proximity a role in topic learning alongside the observed text. The authors also motivate the approach through efficient methods for computing optimal-transport distances and the need to handle both long and short documents within a common framework.

Experiments across assorted text corpora show better topic coherence than competitive approaches, covering both document-length regimes. The learned topic representations also improve accuracy on downstream classification tasks, providing an evaluation beyond coherence itself. Together, these findings suggest that embedding-space geometry can improve both the interpretability of discovered themes and the usefulness of document representations derived from them.
neurips-2020-otlda-a-geometry-aware-opti.tldr: OTLDA uses optimal transport over word-embedding geometry to learn more coherent topics and improve downstream text classification.

paragraphs: MARGE learns to generate text by retrieving related documents and using them to reconstruct a target document. The retrieved material can span multiple languages. This creates an unsupervised, multilingual, multi-document paraphrasing objective that offers an alternative to pre-training through masked language modeling.

The authors show that retrieval and reconstruction can be learned jointly from random initialization. The training objective approximately brings together abilities associated with paraphrasing, translation, summarization across documents, and information retrieval. Those connections are noisy rather than exact task supervision, but they allow a single pre-training procedure to develop capabilities useful across different language tasks.

Without additional task-specific training, MARGE achieves strong results on several tasks, including document translation with BLEU scores up to 35.8. Fine-tuning also produces strong performance across discriminative and generative tasks in multiple languages. The authors present this breadth as evidence for an especially general pre-training method. The reported findings show that retrieving related text can support both learning to reconstruct language and transferring the resulting model to varied tasks.
neurips-2020-pre-training-via-paraphrasi.tldr: MARGE jointly learns multilingual retrieval and text reconstruction, enabling strong zero-shot and fine-tuned performance across language tasks.

paragraphs: Automated image augmentation can improve model performance, but searching for augmentation settings can be expensive. Earlier approaches often searched on a smaller proxy task, leaving uncertainty about whether the resulting settings suited the actual task. RandAugment simplifies the search enough to remove the need for that separate proxy.

The authors find that a single parameter jointly controlling augmentation operations can replace searches over many operation-specific settings. Their example reduces the candidate space from 10³² to 10² possibilities. This greatly lowers search cost while retaining the ability to tune augmentation for the task being trained.

Despite the simplification, the method achieves state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet. With EfficientNet-B7, it reaches 84.7% ImageNet accuracy, improving on baseline augmentation and AutoAugment. The same approach also improves COCO object detection over baseline augmentation. These results show that a much smaller augmentation search can remain effective across classification and detection, making automated augmentation more practical without requiring the elaborate search spaces used previously.
neurips-2020-randaugment-practical-autom.tldr: RandAugment drastically reduces augmentation search complexity while retaining strong image-classification and object-detection performance.

paragraphs: When an agent cannot observe the true state of its environment, it must use memory and infer hidden information while exploring. General partially observable Markov decision processes can be statistically and computationally difficult to learn. This paper identifies a structured subclass where those broad hardness results still permit sample-efficient reinforcement learning.

The proposed OOM-UCB algorithm addresses finite, episodic, undercomplete POMDPs, where the number of observations exceeds the number of latent states. Exploration remains essential in this setting. The algorithm finds an ε-optimal policy with sample complexity Õ(1/ε²), an optimal dependence on accuracy up to logarithmic factors, while depending polynomially on the other relevant quantities.

The paper additionally provides an algorithm for the special case of deterministic state transitions that is both computationally and statistically efficient. This distinction matters: the general undercomplete result establishes sample efficiency, while the deterministic-transition result explicitly includes computational efficiency. Together, the results show how structural restrictions on partially observable environments can make efficient learning possible despite the difficulty of the unrestricted problem.
neurips-2020-sample-efficient-reinforcem.tldr: OOM-UCB achieves sample-efficient exploration in finite episodic undercomplete POMDPs, with an additional computationally efficient result for deterministic transitions.

paragraphs: Supervised Contrastive Learning adapts batch contrastive learning to use class labels directly. Its objective draws representations of examples from the same class together and separates representations from different classes. This makes class relationships shape the embedding space during training, extending an approach developed for self-supervised representation learning.

The paper examines two versions of the supervised contrastive loss and identifies the stronger formulation. On ImageNet with ResNet-200, it reports 81.4% top-1 accuracy, exceeding the best previously reported result for that architecture by 0.8 percentage points. It also reports consistent improvements over cross-entropy on other datasets and two ResNet variants.

The benefits extend beyond the main accuracy result. The loss improves robustness to natural corruptions, is more stable across optimizer and augmentation settings, and substantially outperforms cross-entropy in reduced-data experiments. These findings support label-informed contrastive training as a useful alternative objective for supervised image learning. The contribution combines a simple-to-implement loss with evidence that organizing representations by class can improve several aspects of model behavior.
neurips-2020-supervised-contrastive-lear.tldr: Supervised contrastive learning uses labels to organize embeddings by class, improving reported accuracy, corruption robustness, and training stability.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks use relationships between examples, but a suitable input graph may be unavailable or corrupted by adversarial changes. This paper develops a probabilistic framework for learning under both circumstances. It treats graph structure as something to infer jointly with the network rather than requiring it to be fully supplied.

The model combines a prior distribution over graphs with a likelihood defined through a graph convolutional network. A stochastic variational inference algorithm estimates the graph posterior and network parameters together. Because graph-related latent variables are discrete, the method uses continuous Concrete relaxations to propagate gradients through their sampled values during optimization.

Experiments on real datasets examine semi-supervised classification with missing graph data and with adversarially perturbed network structure. The authors show that their method can outperform state-of-the-art Bayesian and non-Bayesian graph-network approaches in these settings. The contribution is a unified way to learn uncertain graph structure and a predictor together, extending where graph convolution can be applied and improving robustness in the evaluated attack settings.
neurips-2020-variational-inference-for-g.tldr: A variational framework jointly infers graph structure and GCN parameters for classification without supplied graphs or under adversarial graph perturbations.

paragraphs: This paper learns continuous-time dynamical models from noisy time-series measurements. Its target is a generalized Hamiltonian decomposition of ordinary differential equations. Alongside the model describing how the system changes, the method learns a scalar energy function, giving the learned dynamics an explicit physics-inspired form.

That form allows strong, high-level prior assumptions to constrain the governing equations. The aim is therefore not only to fit observed trajectories, but to express predictions through a structured description of a general dynamical system. The authors also show how their formulation extends and brings together earlier deep-learning approaches that incorporate physics-inspired priors.

A second contribution is a method for learning continuous-time models from the weak form of the governing equations. The authors describe this approach as less computationally demanding than standard adjoint methods. Together, the contributions address both what structure a dynamical model should learn and how to train it. The result is a framework that jointly learns dynamics and energy while providing a less costly route to continuous-time model fitting.
neurips-2020-weak-form-generalized-hamil.tldr: The method jointly learns continuous-time dynamics and an energy function from noisy measurements, using weak-form equations to reduce training cost.
